title: Kelvin Water Dropper Tour
description: Guided walkthrough of induction charging, the positive-feedback loop that makes the dropper interesting, and the spark that ends each cycle.

steps.title: Falling water, rising volts
steps.body: Two streams of water fall through two metal rings into two buckets. There is no battery, no belt, and nothing rubbing against anything — the only energy source is gravity pulling the drops down. Kelvin called it a 'water-dropping influence machine' in 1867.

steps.title: Step 1 — charging by induction
steps.body: Each ring is wired to the *opposite* bucket. A ring at a slightly negative potential repels electrons out of the water passing through it, so the drop pinches off carrying a positive charge — and lands in the bucket that makes the other ring more negative still. No contact, no rubbing: the charge is induced.

steps.title: Step 2 — the positive-feedback loop
steps.body: More charge in a bucket means a stronger ring field, which means more charge on the next drop. The plant integrates exactly that: dV/dt carries a term proportional to V itself. A tiny seed imbalance — thermal noise, in the real apparatus — is enough to start it, and the voltage then climbs roughly exponentially rather than linearly.

steps.title: Step 3 — what sets the ceiling
steps.body: Two things fight the climb: leakage bleeding charge away, and the rising field pushing back on drops that are trying to fall into a bucket already at their own polarity. Watch the particle stream slow and wander as the voltage readout rises — the drops are doing work against the field they built.

steps.title: Step 4 — breakdown, and start again
steps.body: When the gap field passes the classroom air-breakdown estimate (~3×10⁶ V/m) the plant fires a spark and dumps most of the stored charge. The voltage collapses, the loop restarts from near zero, and the cycle repeats — the sawtooth in the readout is the whole machine in one trace.

steps.title: What this model is not
steps.body: A single lumped voltage state with a feedback term, a leak term and a breakdown threshold. No drop-by-drop charge accounting, no electrostatic field solve, no humidity, and no shared charge bus with the Van de Graaff — the two electrostatic devices stay separate models here. Classroom numbers, not metrology.
